en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Mother Deer, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Buddha said: "In the past, there was a herd of several hundred deer that followed the lush grass and drew near to human habitation."
In a certain town, the king went out on a hunt, and the deer were scattered in all directions.
There was a doe who was pregnant; she fled alone, pursued by hunters, exhausted by hunger and deprived of her companions, filled with grief and distress.

At that time, she gave birth to two fawns and left them to go in search of food. Left solitary and trembling with fear, she lost her composure and fell into a hunter’s snare. She cried out piteously, wishing to escape, but could not free herself.
Hearing the sound, the hunter went to investigate; seeing the deer, he was pleased and moved forward, intending to kill it.
The deer then bowed its head in supplication, pleading for mercy and explaining:

"I have recently given birth to two fawns who are still small and ignorant. They can only gaze blankly, not yet knowing east from west. I beg you to grant me a brief moment to return and see my offspring, to show them where to find water and grass so they may survive. I shall return immediately to face death, never failing my solemn vow."
At that time, the hunter, hearing what the deer said, was struck with wonder and found it most extraordinary!
He immediately replied to the deer, saying:
"If even all the people of the world lack ultimate sincerity, how much more so you, a deer?"
“Once you have departed from death, how could there be a time for your return?
I shall never let you go.
The deer replied again:

"If you listen to me, my son will survive; if you do not, my son will perish. If mother and son both die, we shall not be able to part while alive. It would be better to share our death to preserve my son, for the three kinds of agony would otherwise be most intense.
She then spoke a verse to address the hunter:
"My body is that of a beast, Roaming through the forests and thickets."
In my lowly life, I clung greedily to body and life, unable to face death with composure.
Now I have entered your snare and am destined for the butcher's block;
I do not begrudge this foul-smelling carcass, but I pity my two children alone.
At this, the hunter heard what the deer said; it was most strange and marvelous!
Yet his mind still harbored greed, so he replied to the deer:

"Deceitful artifice is without substance, and the treacherous are difficult to trust. Empty flourishes are manifold and guileful schemes are not of one kind. Few who cherish their own bodies and dread death are able to sacrifice their lives; since a person of no integrity is already hard to rely upon, how much more so a wild beast—once gone, will it ever return?"
"I shall certainly not let you go; there is no need for further stratagems.
The deer again shed tears and replied with a verse:
"Though my body is that of a lowly beast, I am ignorant of human propriety and righteousness."
Alas, how can I receive your compassionate grace, only to depart once and never return?
I would rather endure the agony of being torn asunder than exist in hypocrisy;
grieving for my two children’s wretched plight, I beg for a brief moment of leave.
If there are evil people in the world who incite strife and disorder among the bhikṣu-saṃgha,
destroy stūpas and ruin Buddhist temples, kill arhats,
commit rebellion by harming their parents, or harm their brothers and wives;
"If I do not return, my transgression will be greater than this.
At that time, the hunter heard the deer's words again; his heart was filled with even greater trepidation, and he sighed in lamentation: "Alas!

Though I have been born as a human being in this world, I am deluded and ignorant, dark and blind. I turn my back on gratitude and lack righteousness, making it my profession to harm sentient beings through hunting and killing. Deceitful and seeking gain by any means, I am greedy and shameless, unaware of impermanence and unable to distinguish the Three Honored Ones."
"The words of this deer differ from those of humans; its sincere vow is far-reaching, and its feelings are manifest within its very heart.
He then stepped forward, untied the snare, and released it so that the deer might depart.
Thereupon, the mother deer went to her son's side; bowing her head and lowing plaintively, she licked his body, feeling both sorrow and joy, and spoke these verses:
"All meetings with those one loves arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions;
where there is meeting, there is separation, for that which is impermanent cannot endure long."
"Now I am your mother, / Constantly fearing I shall not preserve myself;
/ In this world there is much dread, / For life is as precarious as morning dew.
Then the doe, leading her two fawns to show them good water and grass, shed a torrent of tears and spoke these verses:
"I went out this morning and met with misfortune; By mistake, I fell into the hands of a hunter.
I should have been slaughtered and dismembered, My body crushed and reduced to decay."
"I remember how you came seeking my compassion; now you must return to face death.
I pity that you were orphaned so young; strive with all your might to sustain yourself.
Having spoken thus, the mother deer departed.
The two children cried out and wept piteously, longing for her as they pursued her from behind, falling to the ground and rising again.
Their mother looked back and commanded them, saying:
"Return! Do not come after me!"
Do not let mother and child perish together.
I would die with a willing heart;
it is only that I grieve for you, not yet understanding that in this world, impermanence brings separation to all.

"I am myself of meager fortune and you have been born with scant blessings; why do you pity me? It only serves to increase our grief and affliction. You should simply establish yourself in practice to exhaust your karmic offenses.
Thereupon, the mother again spoke these verses for her son:
"In my previous life I was greedy and attached, And now I have come to this animal body."
All who are born must die; none can escape the suffering that ends with life.
By restraining the mind and severing greed, one thereafter attains great peace.
It is better to die with sincerity and faith than to live a life of deceit and peril.
"The son continued to wail in grief and pursue his longing for his father, traveling as far as the great hunting nets to search for him here and there.
There he saw a hunter lying beneath a tree."
The mother deer stood before him and spoke these verses to awaken him:
"The deer I previously released has now returned to face death;
This ignorant and lowly creature of affection has been able to see her two children and bid them farewell."
"As I am about to depart, I show you water and grass, and for your sake, I speak of impermanence and suffering.
Even if I perish ten thousand times, I shall have no regrets; mindful of your kindness, I dare not betray it.
At this, the hunter suddenly woke up and started in alarm. The deer knelt again before the hunter and spoke these verses once more:
“‘Having been released by you just now, my virtue surpasses that of heaven and earth;
though a lowly beast, I have been nurtured with compassion, and having fulfilled my word, I return to face death.’”
"Moved by your benevolence, which is difficult to forget, I dare not disobey your command.
Though I harbor a thousandfold desire to repay you, I shall still not be able to exhaust my record of gratitude.

When the hunter saw that the deer was so steadfast in its faith and died for the sake of righteousness—its will and integrity being so sincere and its compassionate conduct arising from within—and witnessed the efficacy of its vow as it sacrificed its life to fulfill its oath, he followed after them, drawn by the mutual sorrow and longing between mother and child.
Moved by compassion and pity, he bowed his head in apology and said:
"Since you are a deity of heaven and the earth, and your integrity and righteousness are so sublime, my heart is filled with awe and trepidation;
how could I dare to commit an act of rebellion or harm against you?"
"I would rather kill my own kin, shatter my body along with my wife and children,
than how could I bear to harm a sacred spirit by giving rise to even a hair’s breadth of such a thought?
The hunter immediately released the deer and let it go.
The mother and son, their voices crying out with a mixture of grief and joy, offered this verse of thanks to the hunter:
"Though we are lowly beasts living in this world, We ought to have been filled for the kitchen.
Yet you have immediately divided us for cooking; Out of great kindness, you have spared our two children."
"The Heavenly Benevolence values all things with deep affection, and I have further been granted the grace of release and pardon.
The accumulated blessings of such virtue are immeasurable, beyond what words can describe.

At that time, the hunter reported this in full to the King. The people of the kingdom all came to know of it and were universally moved by his compassionate faith; seeing that the deer’s benevolent conduct was consistent with righteousness, there was none who did not solemnly admire him.
To bring an end to the killing of the hunt, the deer returned to their herd and called out to their companions; they wandered and gathered together, each finding peace in its own place.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In the past, I underwent such diligent suffering as this.
At that time, the deer was my own self;
the two sons were Rāhula and the Arhat Cūḍapanthaka."
The king of that country was Śāriputra. The hunter at that time was you yourself.

When I entered that realm to promote the flourishing of the Way and its transformation, I sowed seeds of goodness without weariness and bestowed merit without dwelling upon it. Although I was among birds and beasts, I did not forget my bodhisattva resolve; I acted with skillful means as appropriate to guide and benefit all, universally enabling sentient beings to cross over, be saved, and attain peace. By means of these merits, one swiftly achieves the state of a Buddha, a True Person. One must practice with utmost sincerity, loyalty, and faith; this is something that cannot but be done.
The Sūtra on the Mother Deer Spoken by the Buddha.
